title: Théorie des cycles algébriques : conjectures de Hodge, Tate, Lefschetz, Weil : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
Context, reconstructed from this page and its neighbours. This reading is an interpretation, not settled. N is the dimension of a singular, probably local, object X, best read as an isolated singularity: the spectrum, or punctured spectrum, of a complete or henselian local ring, or a cone. Y is a general hyperplane section through the singular point, of dimension N-1. A^i denotes local Chow-type groups. Each A^i is split into a 'continuous' part J^i (intermediate-Jacobian or Picard-variety type) and a 'discrete' part N^i (Néron–Severi type, cycles modulo algebraic equivalence). 'exc. p' means 'except for p-torsion' in characteristic p.

The programme on the previous and next pages is a local Lefschetz theory for all codimensions:
- A^i(X)->A^i(Y) is bijective for small i and injective in the next case.
- The 'critical cases' are i ~ N/2.
- Vanishing statements hold above the middle: A^i(X) is finite for i > N/2. This is an analogue of cohomological dimension and connectivity results for links and punctured spectra.
- One should define local intersection forms on N^i(X).
- One should develop a theory of vanishing cycles for J and N in the critical degrees.

The previous page treats N=2 and identifies 'N^1(X) finite' with a theorem of Mumford(-Hodge). For a normal surface singularity, the discrete part of the local class group is the cokernel of the intersection matrix of the exceptional curves. That matrix is negative definite (Mumford 1961, Grauert), so the cokernel is finite. The 'essential group' there is J^1(X), the continuous part (Pic^0 of a resolution).

This page, N=3:
(1) Conjecture A^2(X) finite, in particular J^2(X)=0. This is the top-range vanishing.
(2) Conjecture J^1(X)->J^1(Y) injective except for p-torsion. This is the local Lefschetz injectivity for the continuous part of the local Picard or class group, cf. SGA2 XI for depth >= 3.
(3) Already contained in (1).
The essential groups are J^1(X) and N^1(X), which together determine A^1(X). The essential homomorphisms are J^1(X)->J^1(Y), together with maps A^1(X)'->J^1(Y) and N^1(X)'->J^1(Y). The primed groups are presumably the subgroups of classes whose restriction to Y lands in the continuous part.

Open problems listed for N=3:
(i) Find a natural complement of J^1(X) inside J^1(Y), corresponding to 'vanishing cycles'.
(ii) Give a meaning to a formula J^1(X) ≅ J^1(Y)^π, with π a monodromy or fundamental group of the family of hyperplane sections. This is an invariant-cycle theorem at the level of cycle groups.
(iii) Reinterpret the Hodge index theorem for projective surfaces as negativity of a form on N^1(X).
Point (iii) makes sense if X is, for example, the 3-dimensional cone over a projective surface S. Then N^1(X) = NS(S)/Z·h. The natural local form, obtained by restricting to the surface section Y and using Mumford's negative form there, becomes the intersection form on primitive classes. Its negativity is exactly the Hodge index theorem. In this way the 3-dimensional local picture generalises Mumford–Grauert negativity from dimension 2.

N=4:
(1) N^2(X) finite and A^3(X) finite, in particular J^3(X)=0.
(2) J^1(X)->J^1(Y) bijective and N^1(X)->N^1(Y) injective (except p), hence A^1(X)->A^1(Y) bijective except p. This is the higher-depth local Lefschetz theorem for local Picard groups that gives Grothendieck's proof of Samuel's conjecture: complete intersections of dimension >= 4 that are factorial in codimension <= 3 are factorial.

The next page continues: for N=4 the essential hom is N^1(X)->N^1(Y), again with a vanishing-cycle complement and N^1(X) ≅ N^1(Y)^π. It then states the general pattern: for N=2m+1, A^i ≡ 0 for i >= m+1; for N=2m, N^m ≡ 0 and A^i ≡ 0 for i >= m+1.
errors: Conjecture (1) for N=3 (A^2(X) finite, J^2(X)=0) cannot hold without strong extra hypotheses if X is allowed to be, e.g., the cone over a smooth surface S of degree >= 4 in P^3. That is an isolated 3-dimensional hypersurface singularity. Its codimension-2 local Chow group contains essentially A_0(S) modulo h·Pic(S). By Mumford (1968) this is infinite-dimensional when p_g(S)>0. So 'fini' must be meant modulo some equivalence, or for special classes of singularities (e.g. rational ones), or for henselian/complete local rings where the issue is subtle and was not settled until much later work on Chow groups of local rings. The page gives no hypotheses.

The roles of the groups are not fully fixed on the page. The meaning of the primed groups A^1(X)', N^1(X)' and of the exponent π is left implicit. The formula J^1(X) ⇉/≅ J^1(Y)^π is explicitly posed as a problem ('Donner un sens'), not a claim.

'Injective exc. p' for J^1 in the N=3 case is stated as a conjecture without proof. In SGA2 the corresponding Picard statements need depth or Lefschetz conditions, and the char-p caveats are not specified here.

ideas.what: Local Lefschetz theorems for Chow-type groups of an isolated singularity versus its hyperplane section, in all codimensions, with bijectivity/injectivity ranges and 'critical cases' near the middle dimension
ideas.modern_name: Grothendieck–Lefschetz / local Lefschetz for Chow groups; local Chow groups of singularities
ideas.usually_credited_to: Codimension 1: Grothendieck SGA2 (1962). Higher codimension: conjectural; global analogues in Hartshorne (1975, Equivalence relations on algebraic cycles...); local Chow groups studied by Fulton, Roberts, Kurano, Srinivas
ideas.where_published: Codimension-1 case in SGA2 Exp. XI; the higher-codimension programme is not, to my knowledge, in Grothendieck's published texts

ideas.what: Splitting local cycle groups into a continuous part J^i and a discrete part N^i ('groupes essentiels') and tracking each separately under restriction to a hyperplane section
ideas.modern_name: Abel–Jacobi/algebraic part vs Néron–Severi part of local Chow groups
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lipman (1969) and Mumford (1961) for surface singularities; general case not standard

ideas.what: Finiteness of N^1 for a 2-dimensional normal singularity via the negative definite intersection form (identified as Mumford/'Mumford-Hodge')
ideas.modern_name: Mumford–Grauert negative definiteness; finiteness of the discrete local class group

ideas.what: Vanishing-cycle complement and invariant-cycle formula at the level of cycle groups: J^1(X) ≅ J^1(Y)^π, N^1(X) ≅ N^1(Y)^π
ideas.modern_name: Local invariant cycle theorem / vanishing cycles (SGA7), transposed to Chow and Néron–Severi groups
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cohomological version: Clemens, Deligne (Weil II), SGA7 (Grothendieck, Deligne, Katz)
ideas.where_published: Cohomological vanishing cycles in SGA7; the cycle-group version does not appear there as far as I know

ideas.what: Hodge index theorem for projective surfaces reinterpreted as negativity of a local intersection form on N^1 of a 3-dimensional (cone) singularity
ideas.modern_name: Higher-dimensional local negativity (analogue of the Mumford–Grauert criterion) / Hodge index via cones
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in work on local intersection theory and the negativity lemma; no clear standard attribution

ideas.what: Local Picard Lefschetz in dimension 4: A^1(X)->A^1(Y) bijective except p
ideas.modern_name: Grothendieck's local Lefschetz / Samuel's factoriality conjecture

missed.claim: A systematic programme of local Lefschetz theorems for higher-codimension Chow groups of isolated singularities. It comes with vanishing above the middle dimension (A^i ≡ 0 for i >= m+1, N^m ≡ 0 in even dimension 2m) and critical cases at the middle. This is a local analogue of Hartshorne's later global conjectures, which as far as I know was never formulated as such in print by Grothendieck.
missed.quote: ① A^2(X) fini en particulier J^2(X)=0 ... ② J^1(X)→J^1(Y) injectif exc. p
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Chow groups of local rings (Kurano, Roberts, Srinivas, Levine) remain largely conjectural. A Lefschetz/vanishing framework with explicit critical cases could organise known results and counterexamples, e.g. cones over surfaces with p_g>0.

missed.claim: A theory of 'vanishing cycles' for local cycle groups: a natural complement of J^1(X) in J^1(Y), resp. of N^1(X) in N^1(Y), and an invariant-cycle formula J^1(X) ≅ J^1(Y)^π.
missed.quote: Pb définir un complémentaire naturel de J^1(X) dans J^1(Y) (correspondant aux "cycles évanescents") Donner un sens à la formule J^1(X)⇉J^1(Y)^π
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: The local invariant cycle theorem is a cohomological statement. A version for Picard and Néron–Severi groups of singularities and their hyperplane sections, i.e. monodromy invariants of class groups, is not a standard result.

missed.claim: The Hodge index theorem for projective surfaces is viewed as the negativity of a local intersection form on N^1 of a 3-dimensional singularity, e.g. the cone over the surface. This would extend Mumford's negative-definiteness for surface singularities to dimension 3.
missed.quote: Interpréter le th. de l'indice de Hodge pour les surfaces projectives en termes de la négativité d'une certaine forme définie sur N^1(X)...?
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This links global positivity (Hodge index, standard conjecture of Hodge type) to local negativity on singularities. That is a natural route toward a local or inductive approach to Hodge-type standard conjectures, a theme of this archive file.

deep.surprise_reason: Programmatic notes rather than results. The codimension-1 parts are SGA2. The higher-codimension local Lefschetz/vanishing programme, the cycle-level vanishing-cycle/invariant-cycle problem, and the reading of Hodge index as local negativity are a coherent unpublished agenda, but only sketched. The N=3 finiteness conjecture appears too strong as stated.
transcription_corrections: Ex N=4 ①: 'λ^3(X) fini' should read 'A^3(X) fini' (script A), consistent with 'en particulier J^3(X)=0'.
'exc. p' / 'exc p' = 'excepté p' (up to p-torsion); the struck word after 'injectif exc.' in ② of N=3 is a cancelled start of 'p...'.
The double arrow in 'J^1(X)⇉J^1(Y)^π' is likely an isomorphism sign '≃', cf. the next page 'N^1(X) ≃ N^1(Y)^π'.
Margin note is probably '[accouplement?] défini sur N^1(X)'; the first word is unclear.
In ①, 'J^2(X)=0': the letter looks like script J; reading is consistent with the parallel 'J^3(X)=0' for N=4.
